strengths: Unified framework handling 7+ diverse audio/music generation tasks within a single architecture, addressing a real practical need
Well-motivated and empirically validated multi-modal input masking strategy with consistent improvements shown across ablations
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple datasets (AudioCaps, VGGSound, V2M, MusicCaps, etc.) with diverse metrics (KL, IS, FAD, PC, FQ) and user studies
Strong competitive or SOTA empirical results across most benchmarks compared to specialized baselines (AudioGen, AudioLDM, Stable Audio, MAGNET)
Valuable dataset contributions: 190K audio captions and 5.7M music captions with promise to open-source
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and well-organized paper structure
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: straightforward application of existing Diffusion Transformers with input-level masking rather than fundamental innovation
Evaluation fairness concerns: different baselines trained on different datasets with unclear data availability; unfair direct comparison in Table 1
Dataset construction bias: automatically generated captions using Qwen2-Audio may propagate model bias; quality control for automatic annotations not discussed
Incomplete ablations: no justification for architectural choices (24 layers, projection design), missing comparison of alternative multi-modal fusion approaches
User study limitations: only 10 judges, 25 samples, no inter-rater agreement metrics, no confidence intervals on results
Computational efficiency not addressed: training requires enormous resources (3 clusters, 8x80GB GPUs, 3.2k GPU hours) with no inference latency analysis compared to baselines
Missing failure analysis: no discussion of failure modes, task-specific limitations, or generalization to unseen modality combinations
Unclear how much improvement comes from novel masking strategy vs. large-scale training and additional data; improvements often incremental rather than breakthrough
Evaluation metric concerns: reliance on pre-trained model-based metrics (VGGish) without discussing potential biases; PQ methodology unclear

strengths: Comprehensive scope: Addresses multi-modal audio generation (text, video, image, audio) within a single unified framework
Extensive experimental evaluation across diverse datasets (AudioCaps, VGGSound, AVVP, MusicCaps, V2M-bench) with multiple metrics and task configurations
Large-scale dataset contribution with ~190K audio captions and 5.7M music captions with new annotations
Reasonable multi-modal masking strategy that enables learning from diverse input combinations
Promise of code and dataset release supports reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Primarily applies existing Diffusion Transformer architectures and standard input masking strategies already extensively studied in vision and NLP; lacks novel architectural or methodological insights

Weak and inconsistent empirical results: AudioX does not consistently outperform baselines across datasets (e.g., AudioLDM-Full-Large and TangoMusic surpass AudioX on multiple AudioCaps benchmarks); no clear superiority demonstrated

Inadequate evaluation methodology: User study limited to 25 samples with insufficient methodological detail; no statistical significance testing reported for any results; heavy reliance on automatic metrics that poorly correlate with human audio quality perception

Insufficient justification of unified approach benefits: Paper fails to clearly demonstrate when and why unified training helps versus task-specific approaches; limited analysis of cross-modal interactions and learning

Unfair baseline comparisons: Baselines are task-specific models rather than unified approaches; different training conditions make direct comparison problematic; no comparison with other multi-modal diffusion or multi-task learning approaches

Incomplete ablation studies: Missing ablations on architectural choices, modality interaction mechanisms, and design decisions beyond mask ratios; Figure 6 only compares single-modality models to unified model without analyzing what cross-modal relationships are learned
Missing computational analysis: No discussion of training time, inference latency, or efficiency trade-offs compared to task-specific models
Reproducibility concerns: Paper marked 'work in progress'; unclear whether large V2M-caps dataset (5M captions) will actually be released; new caption dataset details insufficiently specified

strengths: Unified multi-modal framework successfully handles diverse audio generation tasks (text-to-audio, video-to-audio, image-to-audio, inpainting, completion) with a single model rather than task-specific approaches
Novel multi-modal masked training strategy is well-motivated and convincingly validated through comprehensive ablation studies showing clear improvements over feature masking and no masking baselines

Exceptional breadth of experimental evaluation across 8+ datasets and multiple task types with consistent SOTA or near-SOTA performance across diverse scenarios, demonstrating genuine generalization capability
Large-scale dataset contributions including 190K audio captions from VGGSound and 6M music captions from V2M dataset are valuable resources for the research community
Technically sound approach with correct diffusion formulation, well-described training procedures, and appropriate evaluation metrics validated by user studies with professional raters
Comprehensive ablation studies (mask ratios, strategies, modality combinations) clearly justify design choices and provide actionable insights for practitioners
Strong empirical results with clear improvements in multi-modal settings (Figure 6) demonstrating effective cross-modal information integration and alignment
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty - the core contribution is applying existing Diffusion Transformers to multi-modal audio generation; the novelty is primarily in the application and training strategy rather than fundamental algorithmic advancement

Masking strategy, while empirically effective, lacks deep theoretical justification for why input modality masking specifically enhances cross-modal learning compared to other fusion or alignment approaches
Limited comparison with other recent multi-modal generation frameworks and masking strategies; most baselines are single-task or single-modality methods rather than unified multi-modal approaches
Significant computational cost (3.2k GPU hours on 3 H800s) not fully discussed or compared against baselines; missing analysis of inference time and memory efficiency
Insufficient analysis of failure modes, challenging input combinations, and cross-modal conflicts (e.g., misaligned text-video prompts); limited discussion of model limitations

Dataset quality concerns not thoroughly addressed - V2M captions are automatically generated by Qwen2-Audio rather than human-annotated; potential impact of annotation noise on model performance unexplored
Limited evaluation of out-of-domain generalization and systematic analysis of which cross-modal pairs generalize better; image-to-audio generation mentioned but not explicitly evaluated

Motivation for why masking specifically improves multi-modal alignment could be more theoretically grounded rather than purely empirical; connection between information scarcity and improved representation learning needs clarification

strengths: Well-motivated unified framework that addresses a real limitation in existing audio generation models by supporting diverse input modalities (text, video, audio)
Substantial dataset contribution (IF-caps with 7+ million samples) with thoughtfully designed structured annotations and multi-stage curation pipeline
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse tasks (T2A, T2M, V2A, inpainting, completion) with both objective and subjective metrics, showing consistent strong performance
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 3-4) systematically validating design choices and demonstrating the effectiveness of key components like MAF
Discovery of interesting cross-modal regularization effect showing that unified training improves fine-grained instruction-following capability
Strong instruction-following performance compared to baselines, demonstrating practical utility
Commitment to releasing code and datasets for community reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty - core components (DiT, diffusion models, cross-attention) are well-established; MAF module is a relatively straightforward combination of standard techniques without significant innovation
Dataset quality concerns due to heavy reliance on LLM-generated annotations (Gemini and Qwen2-Audio) without thorough quality validation, inter-annotator agreement analysis, or error rate reporting
Evaluation methodology limitations including potential circular dependency where LLMs are used for both annotation (Step 1) and judgment (Step 2) of T2A-bench, introducing bias
Insufficient analysis of why design choices are optimal - e.g., why this specific MAF architecture over alternatives, and mechanistic explanation of cross-modal regularization effect
Incomplete failure analysis with no discussion of failure modes, challenging prompt types, or model limitations
Very high computational requirements (3 H800 clusters for ~4k GPU hours) limit reproducibility; inference cost not discussed
Data contamination risks from using public web videos/audio not adequately addressed; potential overlap with test sets not thoroughly analyzed
Limited scope of generalization analysis - all experiments confined to audio/music domains; sensitivity to caption quality not systematically studied

strengths: Large-scale dataset contribution (IF-caps with 7M+ samples) with structured annotation pipeline is valuable for the community
Comprehensive evaluation methodology across multiple metrics, tasks, and datasets with systematic ablation studies
Solid engineering work demonstrating that a unified model can handle multiple audio generation modalities reasonably well
Detailed implementation details and promise to release code/datasets support reproducibility
Introduction of T2A-bench benchmark for instruction-following evaluation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core components (DiT, diffusion, cross-attention) are well-established, and MAF module is a straightforward application of gating and attention mechanisms without significant innovation

Heavy reliance on LLM-generated annotations (Gemini 2.5 Pro) for dataset construction without sufficient quality control, validation, or analysis of potential biases introduced by LLM-generated captions
User study is statistically underpowered (only 10 experts, 25 samples per task) and lacks significance testing; over-reliance on IS metric which is known to be problematic
Modest improvements over baselines in many cases (e.g., IS of 1.27 vs 1.29 on VGGSound), and unclear whether improvements stem from architectural changes, the large dataset, or training procedures
Missing critical analysis including: failure case examination, computational cost comparison, modality contribution analysis, and systematic investigation of what the model struggles with
Overclaimed novelty: presented as a 'unified' solution but is fundamentally a standard multi-input diffusion model; improvements are often incremental rather than substantial
Insufficient evidence for claimed 'cross-modal regularization effect' and lack of rigorous justification for specific architectural design choices
No validation of LLM-generated data quality against human annotations, and limited discussion of potential systematic biases from LLM-based augmentation strategy

strengths: Addresses a genuine problem: unified framework for diverse audio generation tasks from flexible multimodal inputs (text, video, audio combinations)
Significant dataset contribution: IF-caps with 7+ million audio-music samples and fine-grained structured annotations, addressing a key bottleneck in audio generation research
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 7+ benchmarks (T2A-bench, T2A, V2A, TV2A, T2M, V2M, T2M/TV2M) with diverse metrics and user study validation with 10 professional audio experts
Strong empirical results, particularly impressive on instruction-following (T2A-bench), substantially outperforming all baselines
Well-designed MAF module effectively addresses multimodal fusion challenges through gating, learnable cross-attention queries, and self-attention consolidation; ablations validate each component
Thorough technical soundness with proper mathematical formulations, clear implementation details, and systematic ablation studies validating design choices
Clear presentation with well-motivated problem statement, effective figures, and comprehensive appendix supporting reproducibility
High practical impact: unified framework has immediate applications in content creation and multimedia production; if released, dataset will be valuable for the community
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: core components (DiT, diffusion, cross-attention) are established; MAF module, while useful, is relatively straightforward gating and attention mechanisms without fundamental new insights
Primarily an engineering contribution combining existing techniques rather than introducing novel methods, limiting technical conceptual advances

Incomplete comparative analysis: some improvements are marginal (e.g., V2A results show near-ties with baselines); strongest advantages on T2A-bench which is a custom benchmark designed by authors; unclear if baselines trained on equivalent datasets
Missing computational analysis: no discussion of training time, inference latency, or model size compared to specialized models, important for practitioners
Limited failure analysis and discussion of limitations: paper lacks scenarios where unified approach might underperform specialized models or when the framework breaks down
Evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no error bars or significance testing reported, only point estimates provided
Data composition unclear: exact task-specific training data composition not always explicit; zero-padding strategy for missing modalities needs better explanation
Cross-modal regularization effect (Sec. 5.4) is relatively intuitive finding; limited technical insights about how different modalities interact beyond validation that high-quality text helps
